title: Adonijah Asked to Marry Abishag—and Solomon Had Him Killed
paragraphs:
Adonijah Asked to Marry Abishag—and Solomon Had Him Killed
The request sounded like romance. Solomon heard a claim to the throne. And buried inside this disturbing royal scandal is a warning about the desires we keep renaming instead of surrendering—and a Gospel truth about the King who does not merely expose rebels, but saves them.
There are Bible stories we soften because the unfiltered version makes us uncomfortable.
This is not one of those stories.

An aging king lies weak in his bed. A beautiful young woman is brought into the royal chamber to care for him. A prince declares himself king before his father is even dead. Another son is crowned instead. The defeated prince runs terrified to the altar and grabs its horns, begging for his life.
He is spared.
Then he makes one more request.
He wants the woman who had lain beside his father.
And shortly afterward, Solomon orders his execution.
Read that too quickly and Solomon can seem terrifyingly insecure.
Slow down.
Because Adonijah was not simply asking for a wife.
He was reaching toward something he had already tried to take.
A kingdom.
And before we judge him from a comfortable distance, Scripture quietly turns the mirror toward us.
Because sometimes the most dangerous desires in your heart are not the ones you openly call sin.
They are the ones you have learned to make sound innocent.
The story begins in the shadow of David's death.
First Kings 1 describes David as old and unable to keep warm. His servants searched Israel for a beautiful young virgin who could attend him, and they found Abishag of Shunem.
The Hebrew introduces her as:
“אֲבִישַׁג הַשּׁוּנַמִּית” — Avishag ha-Shunammit
“Abishag the Shunammite.”
She cared for David and lay beside him to keep him warm, while the biblical narrator explicitly tells us that David did not have sexual relations with her.
Then, almost immediately, Scripture moves to Adonijah.
And the first words describing what happens inside him are revealing.
“וַאֲדֹנִיָּה בֶן־חַגִּית מִתְנַשֵּׂא לֵאמֹר אֲנִי אֶמְלֹךְ”
Va’Adoniyyah ven-Chaggit mitnasse lemor, ani emlokh.
In context:
“Adonijah son of Haggith exalted himself, saying, ‘I will be king.’”
—1 Kings 1:5
That phrase matters.
He exalted himself.
Before Adonijah ever asked for Abishag, Scripture had already exposed the deeper problem.
He wanted elevation.
He wanted the throne.
He wanted what he believed should belong to him.
And the chilling sentence was only three Hebrew words:
“אֲנִי אֶמְלֹךְ”
Ani emlokh.
“I will be king.”
Not, “If God wills.”
Not, “If my father appoints me.”
Not, “If the Lord has chosen me.”
“I will be king.”
That is where the scandal really begins.
Not with Abishag.
With self-exaltation.

Adonijah gathered chariots, horsemen, and fifty men to run before him. He secured the support of Joab and Abiathar. He held a sacrificial feast and invited royal sons and influential men—but conspicuously excluded Solomon, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah, and others loyal to David.
This was not an innocent family celebration.
Adonijah was positioning himself as king.
But David had not crowned him.
God had not appointed him.
And the throne would go to Solomon.
When David learned what was happening, Solomon was publicly anointed and proclaimed king. The celebration was so loud that the earth seemed to shake with the sound.
Adonijah's feast collapsed.
Imagine the scene.
One moment people are eating around the man they expect to rule Israel.
Then news arrives.
Solomon has been crowned.
Suddenly the guests disappear.
Political confidence becomes panic.
Friends become distance.
Celebration becomes survival.
And Adonijah runs.
He takes hold of the horns of the altar.
The man who had announced, “I will be king,” is now begging the actual king not to kill him.
And Solomon does something remarkable.
He gives Adonijah a chance to live.
“If he will show himself a worthy man, not one of his hairs shall fall to the earth.”
—1 Kings 1:52
Adonijah had reached for Solomon's throne.
Solomon nevertheless allowed him to go home.
Mercy had entered the story.
Remember that.
Because what happens next makes no sense unless you remember that Adonijah had already attempted to seize royal authority.
David dies.
Solomon's reign is established.
Then Adonijah approaches Bathsheba, Solomon's mother.
He begins carefully.
“You know that the kingdom was mine, and that all Israel fully expected me to reign.”
Stop there.
Even after everything that happened, Adonijah is still talking about the kingdom as though it had somehow belonged to him.
Yes, he acknowledges that it turned to Solomon and says it came from the LORD.
But then comes the request.
He asks Bathsheba to speak to Solomon on his behalf:
“Please ask King Solomon—he will not refuse you—to give me Abishag the Shunammite as my wife.”
—1 Kings 2:17
At first glance, it can sound almost heartbreakingly simple.
A defeated prince wants a woman.
Maybe he loves her.
Maybe he is lonely.
Maybe Solomon overreacts.
Except the text never tells us Adonijah loved Abishag.
Not once.
We should be careful not to manufacture a romance Scripture never gives us.
And Solomon certainly did not interpret the request as merely romantic.
When Bathsheba presents it, Solomon responds:
“Why do you ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Ask for him the kingdom also…”
—1 Kings 2:22
That sentence unlocks the scene.
Why would marrying Abishag have political significance?

Because in the ancient royal world, possession of a deceased or displaced king's concubine or woman associated with his royal household could function as a public claim to royal succession or authority.
The Bible itself gives us disturbing examples.

When Absalom rebelled against David, he publicly went in to David's concubines in Jerusalem. It was not merely sexual immorality. It was a calculated political declaration that David's authority had been displaced.
Earlier, Ish-bosheth reacted fiercely when Abner was accused of sleeping with Saul's concubine Rizpah. The accusation carried implications far beyond private romance.

So when Adonijah—the man who had already attempted to become king—asked for the young woman intimately associated with David's final royal household, Solomon heard something Bathsheba apparently did not immediately treat as an explicit coup.
A renewed claim.
A throne-shaped desire wearing the clothes of marriage.
And Solomon had Adonijah executed.
The text is severe.
It should feel severe.
We do Scripture no favors by pretending otherwise.
But we also do Scripture no favors by ripping one execution out of its political and narrative setting and presenting Solomon as murdering a harmless lovesick brother.
Adonijah was not an anonymous citizen who unexpectedly fell in love.

He was a rival claimant who had previously proclaimed himself king, assembled powerful supporters, held what functioned as a coronation feast, received mercy after his failed attempt, and then sought Abishag.
Solomon interpreted the request alongside the continuing danger represented by Adonijah, Abiathar, and Joab.
First Kings 2 subsequently narrates Solomon removing those threats as his kingdom is consolidated.
And then Scripture says:
“So the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon.”
—1 Kings 2:46
But there is something even more uncomfortable here.
Something much closer to us.
Adonijah's tragedy did not begin when Benaiah came through the door.
It began when a man decided:
“I will be king.”
And suddenly this ancient royal scandal becomes painfully modern.
Because there is an Adonijah-shaped temptation hiding inside the human heart.
Maybe you have never wanted a literal throne.
But have you ever wanted control?
Have you ever known what God said…and quietly decided you wanted something else?
Have you ever prayed for God's will while secretly demanding your own?
Have you ever called something “love” because admitting it was lust would hurt?
Called it “discernment” because admitting it was jealousy would embarrass you?
Called it “protecting my peace” when you were actually refusing to forgive?
Called it “ambition” when your identity was starving for applause?
Called it “waiting for the right time” when you were simply refusing to obey?
Called it “just one more time” while knowing exactly where the road was taking you?
That is where this story stops being ancient history.
Because sin rarely walks into our lives introducing itself honestly.
It negotiates.
It renames itself.
It explains itself.
It puts respectable clothing around rebellion.
And eventually we can become so skilled at explaining our desires that we stop asking the most frightening question:
Does Jesus actually have permission to say no to me?
Not merely to your pornography.
Not merely to your affair.
Not merely to your addiction.
Not merely to obvious rebellion.
Your plans.
Your relationships.
Your money.
Your reputation.
Your anger.
Your sexuality.
Your ambitions.
Your grudges.
Your future.
Your secret fantasies about who you deserve to become.
Your need to be recognized.
Your need to win.
Your need to have the last word.
Your throne.
Because Christianity is not adding Jesus to a kingdom where you remain sovereign.
Jesus is King.
That is the collision at the center of discipleship.
Adonijah said:
“I will be king.”
The Gospel announces:
Jesus is Lord.
The Greek confession carried by the earliest Christians is breathtakingly short:
“Κύριος Ἰησοῦς Χριστός”
Kyrios Iēsous Christos.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
Paul writes that one day every knee will bow and every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
That means the central question of your life is ultimately not whether you consider Jesus useful.
It is whether you will surrender.
And here the story becomes infinitely more beautiful than Adonijah's.
Because we have rebelled against a King too.
We have reached for God's authority.
We have wanted His gifts without His rule.
We have sinned.
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
—Romans 3:23
But the greater Son of David did something Solomon never did for Adonijah.
Jesus took the judgment of rebels upon Himself.
Read that again.
Adonijah reached for a throne and died.
We reached for God's throne—
and the King came down from His.
Christ did not die because Rome accidentally defeated Him.
He gave Himself.
At the cross, the sinless Son of God bore sin so guilty people could be reconciled to God.
Paul writes:
ton mē gnonta hamartian
The One “who knew no sin.”
God made Him to be sin for us, “so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.”
—2 Corinthians 5:21
This is the scandal of grace.
The rightful King dies for rebels.
The Holy One bleeds for sinners.
The Judge bears judgment.
The Shepherd dies for wandering sheep.
The Son receives nails while His enemies are offered adoption.
Jesus does not look at our rebellion and pretend it was harmless.
Grace is not God lowering His definition of holiness until everybody qualifies.
Grace is infinitely more costly than that.
At Calvary, God demonstrates both the horror of sin and the immeasurable depth of His love.
The cross tells you:
Your sin is worse than your excuses admit.
And God's grace is greater than your shame can imagine.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Something you do not want Jesus touching.
Something you keep asking Him to bless without ever asking whether He wants you to surrender it.
Your Abishag.
Not necessarily a person.
A desire.
A secret.
A compromise.
A throne.
And perhaps the Holy Spirit is pressing the question into your conscience:
Why are you still reaching for what you already surrendered?
Adonijah received mercy after his first rebellion.
Then he reached again.
Do not confuse God's patience with God's approval.
Scripture says God's kindness is meant to lead us toward repentance.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
The New Testament word is:
“μετάνοια”
metanoia.
It speaks of repentance—a changed mind and turning reflected in a changed direction.
Biblical repentance is not self-hatred.
It is turning from sin toward God.
It is finally stopping the negotiation.
No more renaming.
No more hiding.
No more explaining why everybody else is responsible.
No more asking Jesus to be Savior while politely refusing His kingship.
You can come into the light.
Not because your sin does not matter.
Because Christ's blood does.
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9
There is forgiveness.
There is cleansing.
There is restoration.
There is a way home.
Peter denied Jesus and was restored.
Paul persecuted Christians and became an apostle of Christ.
The thief beside Jesus had nothing left to offer Him but faith and a dying confession—and Jesus promised him paradise.
That is our theme because that is the heartbeat of the Gospel:
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By redeeming the sinner inside it.
Maybe your story contains chapters you wish you could tear out.
Sexual sin.
Infidelity.
Addiction.
Pride.
Greed.
Abuse you inflicted.
Words you cannot retrieve.
Years you wasted.
Faith you abandoned.
People you wounded.
Promises you broke.
Secret things nobody knows.
Jesus does not need an edited version before you approach Him.
Bring the truth.
Bring the wreckage.
Bring the shame.
Bring the throne you have been defending.
Repent and believe the Gospel.
Because Jesus Christ did not rise from the dead merely to make slightly nicer versions of rebels.
He came to make us new.
Be honest.

And if Christ has already brought you through something you once thought would destroy your faith, tell part of your testimony. Somebody reading the comments may desperately need evidence that failure does not have to write the final chapter when Jesus enters the story.
Not because every sentence will feel comfortable tomorrow.
Because some truths need to be reread precisely when they become uncomfortable.
Not as a religious badge. Not to prove you are more spiritual than anyone else. Somebody may have been asking God for one interruption before walking deeper into compromise.
Supporting Gospel work can be one genuine way to steward resources for God's glory when it is done freely, wisely, and from the heart. We will never turn grace into a transaction.
And there is much more available without payment.
Jesus is calling sinners home.
Adonijah's story asks what happens when a man keeps reaching for a throne that is not his.
The Gospel asks a more personal question:
What are you still gripping that belongs under the lordship of Christ?
Maybe tonight your greatest act of worship will not be singing louder.
Maybe it will be opening your hand.
Confessing the sin.
Ending the compromise.
Making the apology.
Deleting the secret.
Walking away.
Coming home.
Not because surrender purchases grace.
Because grace has finally shown you that Jesus is better than the throne you were destroying yourself trying to keep.
The throne was never going to save you.
The secret was never going to heal you.
The applause was never going to satisfy you.
The sin was never going to keep its promises.
But Christ—
crucified for sinners,
risen from the dead,
full of grace and truth—
still receives those who come to Him.

Invite your family, your struggling Christian friend, the believer who has grown cold, the seeker with questions, and even the unbeliever who thinks grace could never possibly have room for someone like them.
The most dangerous throne may be the one hidden inside your heart—but the hands asking you to surrender it are the same hands that were pierced to bring you home.
